newsitem.title: MEXICO: Poison, prison and bullets - the drug lord's fate.
newsitem.headline: Poison, prison and bullets - the drug lord's fate.

text.p: Some went out with a bang, others with a whimper, but Latin America's drug lords have rarely exited the stage in the style to which they were accustomed.
As one U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agent with long service in Latin America put it:
"If you're a major drug trafficker, you're not going to be sitting on a ranch somewhere with grandchildren on your knee -- it's a very short-term livelihood."

Billionaire Mexican cocaine king Amado Carrillo Fuentes' ignominious death in a hospital bed last week might rank as the weirdest exit by a reigning capo -- especially if reports that he was killed by an overdose of medicine slipped into his intravenous drip prove true.
Carrillo Fuentes died amid bawling babies and pregnant women in a mostly maternity hospital after a lengthy plastic surgery and liposuction operation to disguise his appearance.
Colombia's greatest drug lord, Medellin cartel boss Pablo Escobar, also looked dramatically different from archive photographs when he met his end in his home city in December 1993.
But at least Escobar went out like a true gangster, cut down by bullets in a rooftop shoot-out with police in hot pursuit.
Officers had intercepted a birthday radiophone call between the boss and his family and used direction-finding equipment to pinpoint the modest house where he was hiding.
Escobar's cartel coined the phrase which epitomised the Colombian narco-traffickers' fear of extradition: "Better a tomb in Colombia than a jail cell in the United States."

Escobar's top lieutenant Gonzalo Rodriguez Gacha -- once Colombia's most feared narco-terrorist after masterminding a string of bombings and assassinations in the late 1980s -- took the refrain to heart.
Rather than allow police closing in from a helicopter in northern Colombia the satisfaction of catching their prey, Gacha held up a grenade, made a V-sign, and blew his own head off.
Fellow Medellin cartel mobster Carlos Lehder was not so lucky -- police caught him alive in February 1987 and packed him off in chains to the United States.

Lehder is now serving a sentence of life without parole plus 135 years -- a fate similar to that of Mexican Gulf Cartel chieftain Juan Garcia Abrego, convicted in a Houston court and sentenced to life without parole after his arrest and deportation from Mexico in 1996.
But other leading capos have proved prison does not have to be a problem -- as long as it's not an American jail you're sent to.

Escobar's partners during the Medellin cartel heyday, the three Ochoa brothers surrendered to police to take advantage of huge sentence reductions offered by Colombian law for traffickers who cooperated with local justice.

The reductions, allied with extra benefits for "good behaviour and study," proved so generous that after less than six years, the Ochoas were released from jail to "retire" and enjoy their multi-million-dollar fortune.
Escobar's brother Roberto, who was imprisoned in the same jail as the Ochoas, didn't have such a good time. A parcel bomb sent by the rival Cali cartel blew up in his face and blinded him.
In a particularly unkind cut, enemies also kidnapped and castrated his favourite prize-winning stallion, whose semen had been worth millions.

Luck ran out for the head of Colombia's other big drug cartel, the Cali mob in June 1995. That was when police found Cali capo Gilberto Rodriguez Orejuela hiding in a small wooden closet. He surrendered without a struggle and even begged police not to shoot.
His brother Miguel was caught in a Cali residence months later and both are now in jail in Colombia -- doubtless hoping for the same leniency shown to the Ochoas.
